record.title: LLM-built simple baselines recover much of published deep-learning gains across 36 scientific prediction tasks
record.summary: An October 28 arXiv preprint reports that one Claude Opus 5 workflow constructed supervised prediction baselines across 36 tasks reconstructed from selected open-access papers in Nature-, Science- and Cell-family journals. Across task medians, the authors report a median simple-baseline strength of 95.5% and a mean of 85.7%; on 12 tasks the median baseline matched or exceeded the published deep-learning score. The result is a bounded author-reported audit of predictive contributions, not evidence that the source studies are invalid or that predictive accuracy captures interpretability or scientific insight.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a median simple-baseline strength of 95.5% and mean of 85.7% across the 36 task medians; 12 task medians matched or exceeded the published deep-learning score.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The task harness kept private test labels and grading data outside the agent container, while task documentation visible to the agent often stated the reported score.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper's results establish that simple baselines routinely invalidate deep-learning contributions across scientific fields or improve peer review outcomes.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the reported 36-task result or a representative subset was found or run in this activation.
The arXiv paper says reproduction code is released, but its linked GitHub page showed only README/LICENSE and a single commit in the inspected rendering.
The paper does not establish how frequently these findings occur across scientific publications or whether automated baseline checks change peer-review outcomes.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported workflow generalizes, low-cost automated baselines could expose overstated predictive gains and widen access to a basic research-quality check across scientific machine learning. The consequence is notable for methodology and evaluation, but the study's limited task/model sample and author-run comparisons do not establish field-wide effects.
limitations: Only 36 supervised tasks from a small, selected set of open-access journals were examined; the study used one model, Claude Opus 5.
Each task used one fold; for 13 multi-fold studies, comparison uses a single published reference score that may summarize several folds.
Task reconstruction may not perfectly match the source study due to unspecified splits, changes in code/data, or curator error.

The model may have seen source papers or datasets during pretraining; task documentation often revealed the published score; the study compares with reported results rather than matched reruns of the deep-learning methods.
SBS depends on the chosen trivial predictor and metric; equal SBS increments need not correspond to equal predictive utility or scientific value.
The linked repository page exposed only README/LICENSE and one commit during inspection; the paper's code-availability claim was not confirmed from visible repository contents.
brief.summary: An October 28 arXiv preprint reports that one Claude Opus 5 workflow constructed supervised prediction baselines across 36 tasks reconstructed from selected open-access papers in Nature-, Science- and Cell-family journals. Across task medians, the authors report a median simple-baseline strength of 95.5% and a mean of 85.7%; on 12 tasks the median baseline matched or exceeded the published deep-learning score. The result is a bounded author-reported audit of predictive contributions, not evidence that the source studies are invalid or that predictive accuracy captures interpretability or scientific insight.

technical.claimed_result: Across 36 selected supervised prediction tasks, five medium-effort single-attempt runs per task using Claude Opus 5 yielded 157 scorable attempts out of 180. The median task-level simple-baseline strength was 95.5% (mean 85.7%); task medians matched or exceeded the published deep-learning score on 12 tasks. Counting unscored attempts as zero lowers the mean to 79.6% while leaving the median at 95.5%.
technical.compute_or_cost: The primary 36-task cohort used five single attempts per task, each with a 30-minute execution cap. A separate nine-task analysis compared longer or iterative test-time compute, but documentation visibility differed across arms and effects were not statistically significant.
technical.demonstrated_result: The source establishes that the authors published a paper describing the task harness and its results; the performance findings remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
technical.implementation_status: A public GitHub repository is linked by the paper, but the repository page inspected in this activation showed one commit and only README/LICENSE; completeness and reproducibility of the released artifact remain unresolved.
technical.mechanism: A language-model agent reconstructs task specifications from published scientific studies, writes and runs a supervised prediction baseline in a sandbox, and submits predictions to an evaluator that keeps test labels and grading data outside the agent container. The authors define simple-baseline strength as the fraction of the published deep-learning method's improvement over a trivial predictor recovered by the baseline.
technical.novelty: A cross-study audit uses an LLM to construct executable simple prediction baselines from published task descriptions and data, with held-out evaluation, and proposes a normalized simple-baseline-strength metric.
technical.regime: Supervised classification and regression on 36 tasks reconstructed from open-access papers published 2024-01-31 through 2026-09-18 in a selected set of Nature-, Science- and Cell-family journals; one Claude Opus 5 model; one fold per task; CPU-only sandbox with a 30-minute per-script cap.
technical.reproducibility: Low pending artifact inspection and independent rerun. The primary findings are one-model author-run results; task reconstruction may be imperfect, the model may have seen source data or papers during pretraining, documentation often disclosed reported scores, and published references were not rerun under matched conditions.
technical.strongest_baseline: The denominator compares an automatically built model with a paper-reported deep-learning score and a defined trivial predictor; the study did not rerun each published method under a matched budget, and the SBS value depends on the trivial predictor and task metric.

brief.title: LLM-built simple baselines recover much of published deep-learning gains across 36 scientific prediction tasks
brief.why_it_matters: If this approach generalizes, inexpensive, executable baseline checks could expose when reported predictive gains rely on weak comparisons and make a basic methodological audit more available to authors and reviewers. The study is bounded to 36 supervised tasks, one model, selected open-access journals, and comparisons against published scores rather than matched reruns, so it does not establish prevalence across science or effects on review outcomes.
